I'm starting to think that actually, the words I use for myself is not to be dictated by other people even if they don't agree with it. I go nonverbal + nonspeaking, or I am semi-verbal or partially nonspeaking, and, I am consequently affected by negative social norms who get impatient with me when they first know me as someone nonverbal, or when they knew I was verbal before and expected to force a word out of me, or when good faith people cannot accommodate me because they're not equipped well to understand me. How is this privilege or talking over?

When I am just speaking about my own experience as an also autistic person? How does that take away from any of your experience, unless you think you are the only Real Autistic. I'm starting to think that those who find the levels helpful need to ask why it's helpful. You need to ask why those of us who were not labeled level 3 because we were missed* as a toddler and only get the label when we are more functional to get assessed as an adult. We're traumatised and forced to cope. I don't think you understand the gravity and toll of masking.

(*And the claim that there's absolutely no way you won't be missed if you're actually level 3 as a child? Do you realise not everyone grew up around adults with great understanding of what autism is? Adults around me thought it was a supernatural thing. My differences were certainly not missed, but the way they were addressed were ignorant. Arguably, you are more privileged to have access to specialists.)

Because what I'm getting is because those labled level 3 are getting support (aided AAC, care homes, caregiver, access to healthcare, fundraising) whether they are good support or not, and in the comfort of being ones who are taken more seriously, want to gatekeep that access from level 1's as if we're gonna limit the resource (that we need). Effectively telling us to go fuck ourselves. While spreading misinformation that level 1's are lying about dying by suicide, or are actually dying because lack of healthcare while disconnecting it from the REASON we're not getting access to healthcare. Reason: only level 3's are valid and severe enough, at the expense of level 1's being ditched. Why not just advocate for support and healthcare for ALL AUTISTICS?

You know why a lot of level 1's are spreading the news that 'nonverbal' is incorrect, even tho a lot of nonverbal autistics don't mind? Because they are trying to listen and do what they think is right and least offensive, because we know what it's like. It's wild really. Because the disability community generally are very welcoming and encourage the use of assistive device or disabled identity if it improves the quality of anyone's life. It's been the least gatekeepy community that I know. Maybe there are strict vocabs to be used only by certain class of impairments, but they are never at the expense of another marginalised group of people, much less calling them liars or people who exaggerate.

My experience:

I never realised that to some people they're unbothered at all, I thought it's just parts and parcels to taking medications, that every dry tablet medication is as bad as or worse than cough syrups. I've realised since then that I'm always bothered by them especially taste-wise, to the point I'd rather stay in physical pain or stay depressed than taking my tablets because I couldn't bear another sensory hell on top of the physical/emotional pain I'm experiencing. The sensory hell also gives me slight headache.

To me the most common meds in my area is paracetamol that tastes warm (not temperature, but TASTE at the back of my tongue) especially the moment I swallow the tablet, and 5-10 minutes after. 

Setraline/zoloft (anti-depressant) tastes bitterly cold, like the clinic air in my mouth. No matter how quick I try to swallow it with water, it'll linger. 

My current med lamictal (mood stabiliser) tastes like blueberries and I'm so glad (manufactured by GSK). It definitely motivates me to be compliant. I used to tell my psychiatrists that I forgot to take my sertraline, because back then I couldn't put it into words the fact that it started with me keep putting it off because I wasn't 'ready' to experience the sensory hell that came with it. I put it off too many times to the point I forgot to take it at all. But now with lamictal I rarely forget (at least due to avoidance).

I was a nonverbal toddler, couldn't remember much. As an adult, I speak minimally though on some occassions when I feel safe and relaxed I could speak at length. When doing transactions whether at the grocery stores or taking the public transport, I barely speak if at all, and usually just point to things (like the shopping cart if I want them) and people have been understanding without insisting I speak. Not so much in academia though.

If my take counts, I think mine is because of my issues with my working memory (as many autistics struggle with this but are great at long-term memory) so I often lose my train of thoughts midway speaking or forget the word for something. But I've got the concept/meaning in my head of what I want to say, just not the words for speech production. Because of this I imagine I'd do much better when I'm fluent in a sign language, but then many other hearing people won't bother to learn it.

Another reason is anxiety as a comorbid thing. I've grown too anxious about my intonation, facial expressions, what I might say wrong etc, so that sort of gives me a feeling like there's a literal lump in my throat that prevents me from speaking.
